children: By Tasha Green Spice

If high-end luxury conglomerates and fast-fashion retailers are at one end of the spectrum, independent brands without corporate overlords are on the other-or on another plane entirely. They fuel appetites for what's new and novel with clothes that are creative, not commercial, a reason that many indie designers are eventually poached to bring their visions to bigger companies.
I speak from experience: In 2008, I had my own indie women's label, Hester, before pivoting to writing, editing and styling.
In a world of algorithm-driven style, discovering an indie brand can be exhilarating. That special moment when you feel like you've found something new, and maybe all your own.

Wearing an indie brand can also show you're in the know. The dozen here, a mix of independent women's and menswear brands, are some of today's most exciting-the ones to watch and shop to keep your style one step ahead.
Donni

Brand bio: Founder Alyssa Wasko Stein worked at Chanel before starting her Los Angeles women's label. It is known for manufacturing close to home and using high-end natural fibers to create sporty basics with a luxurious twist: think taffeta gym shorts and silk track pants.
Notable items: Breezy, pull-on linen pants-basically daytime pajamas-are a popular product. But don't sleep on Donni's loose cotton blouses.

Brand bio: The New York women's label reflects founder Stella Ishii's background running a showroom that has worked with other buzzy independent brands, including The Row and 3.1 Phillip Lim. 6397's head of design, Lizzie Owens, brings a strong men's-wear influence to its collections, which cater to the tastes of the perennial fashion insider with relaxed pieces that have some bite.
Notable items: Reliably a source of good jeans, the brand's other standouts include unfussy silk dresses with a vintage feel.
Cahu

Brand bio: The Parisian accessories company is all about durability without sacrificing design, a philosophy exemplified by its use of PVC, which is also found in bouncy castles. Cahu's eponymous founder, Clémence Cahu, approaches her upscale designs with the rubbery material as if she was using calfskin leather.
Notable items: Cahu's sleek tote bags, available in a range of sizes, strike a balance between utilitarian and high-fashion. Impervious to water and wear, they can take a toddler-level thrashing.
Michelle Del Rio

Brand bio: Designer Michelle Del Rio's namesake women's label, another based in Paris, draws on her Latin-American background. Del Rio's grandmother's favorite boleros, Flamenco dance and milagros charms-metallic tokens featuring religious or other iconography-are among the inspirations for her designs.

Notable items: Pieces like the brand's Ruby jacket-a lightweight coat rendered in crisp cotton that's part Members Only jacket, part billowy dress shirt-pay homage to the cruising culture of Del Rio's native California.
Arma

Brand bio: A new generation is at the helm of the family-run business, founded in 1985, breathing fresh life into its leather and suede goods for women and men. Arma, which has production facilities in Turkey, manufactures for other luxury brands, making it appealing to those who seek quality but who don't want to pay a premium for a status label.

Notable items: Arma's knack for timeless silhouettes with a modern edge is reflected in pieces like its Emy jacket, a sharply tailored, slightly cropped chore coat made of supple lamb's leather in sophisticated earth tones.
Easton Marley

Brand bio: Founders Kendall Marsh and Kylie Mason, both also stylists, are keenly aware of how overwhelming it can be to have too many options. They've intentionally limited the offerings of their Los Angeles women's brand to a handful of hyper-curated clothes and accessories-dresses and sunglasses-inspired by the retro style of their grandmothers.
Notable items: The brand's Odette dress, a drop-waist caftan, channels both bohemian-chic and Old-Hollywood glamour. Its aviator and other sunglasses have a similarly modern-nostalgic spirit.
Glenn's Denim

Brand bio: After 30 years designing, cutting and sewing jeans for others, Glenn Liburd started his namesake New York men's denim label in 2019, at 62-years-old. His products nod to denim as the uniform of American subcultures-from punk to hip-hop-as well as to the 1970s and '80s street style of his youth.
Notable items: Liburd makes jeans in various fits-relaxed, slouchy, straight-using different types of denim. His most-premium styles feature selvage denim woven in America exclusively for his label.
A Day's March

Brand bio: The Swedish label made inroads in the wardrobes of American men and women when it opened its first U.S. store in 2024. That location has since closed, but that hasn't spoiled appetites for the company's streamlined basics, which are manufactured in Portugal and still sold online.

Notable items: Roomy denim and clean knits showcase the brand's Scandinavian sensibility, as do button-up shirts in a pleasing searsucker fabric that makes a subtle statement with checkers, not stripes.
Carter Young

Brand bio: If you're a man who dresses to attract, let Carter Young show you the way. Drawing inspiration from old books and movies, the label's cultivated cool is undeniable. Look no further than the musician George Daniel, who wore a double-breasted, tan suit from the brand at his wedding to the singer Charli XCX last summer.
Notable items: The louche elegance of Carter Young's formal attire also permeates its casual clothes like cotton waffle-knit sweaters and wide-leg chinos, both gateway pieces to nonchalant style.
Bana

Brand bio: Jim and Emily Larsen, the husband and wife behind Bana, are connoisseurs of vintage American men's wear. The couple's obsessive research informs their designs, which are known for thoughtful details-for example, utility shorts with a keychain loop and extra pockets for tools.

Notable items: A bygone swagger permeates the brand's tightly edited collection of blazers, button-down shirts, flared trousers and outerwear like a canvas leisure jacket with an exaggerated collar and curved patch pockets.
Evan Kinori

Brand bio: Founder Evan Kinori designs his men's clothes and accessories in San Francisco, with a slow-fashion philosophy that centers around small-batch production and rigorous fabric selection. Many materials are sourced abroad, from small mills in Belgium, Ireland, Italy and Japan, and feature natural, neutral colors.
Notable Items: Relaxed-fit trousers with an internal elastic waistband and a wide, slightly cropped leg reflect an ease that Kinori also brings to his shirts, shorts and jackets.
Nicholas Daley

Brand Bio: Collaborations with brands like Carhartt WIP and G.H. Bass have widened the spotlight on the Jamaican-Scottish men's wear designer Nicholas Daley, whose reputation has also been burnished by awards from the British Fashion Council and other organizations. His clothes and accessories often feature punchy patterns and bold palettes, bridging the gap between wearable and whimsical.
Notable Items: Pieces like a vibrant hand-crocheted bucket hat, Fair Isle cardigans and Daley's popular Reggae Klub graphic T-shirts showcase the personality he brings to his brand.
